I will keep my land in the usual Quzhou pattern of winter wheat followed by summer maize. In my county, wheat and maize are still the main grain crops, the land is flat, the machinery and inputs are easy to get, and this rotation fits the season well. At my age, I would not spread myself across many crops. I would rather run one simple, familiar system and manage it carefully. Because you did not give my land size, I am assuming I am planning for 10 mu of field land, and I will use the same 10 mu for two crops in one year.

I will sow winter wheat first, then plant summer maize right after wheat harvest. I will use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed because I want stable emergence, uniform stands, and better yield without making management too complicated. I will not push fertilizer too hard. In Quzhou, water is important and fertilizer is often overused, so I will keep nitrogen moderate, add phosphorus and potassium, return straw if I can, and rely on a few key irrigations instead of many. For wheat I will irrigate at the key spring stages, and for maize I will usually give one irrigation if rainfall is not enough. I will keep pesticide use limited to necessary sprays for weeds, diseases, and major insects, because that is simpler and cheaper for me than repeated spraying. For tillage, I will plough before wheat to handle residues and prepare a good seedbed, and I will use no-tillage direct seeding for maize after wheat harvest so I can catch the season quickly.
